headline: September inflation came in hotter than expected at 3.7%, and traders now give the Fed better odds of hiking again on Oct 28.
dateline: Thursday, October 15, 2026 · closes as of Wed Oct 14

rundown.h: Gas did most of the damage in September's CPI.
rundown.p: Energy prices jumped 5.2% in the month, and gasoline is up 34.2% from a year ago. Core prices, which strip out food and energy, rose 0.3%, a tick above the 0.2% forecast, lifting the annual core rate to 2.6% from 2.4%. The Fed's real worry is whether fuel costs start seeping into everything else.

rundown.h: Hike odds for Oct 28 jumped after the report.
rundown.p: Traders lifted the odds of a hike at this month's meeting to about 33%, from about 20% before the data; by Thursday morning they had eased to roughly 27%. New York Fed President John Williams said one more hike may be appropriate this year. A hold is still the base case, but the bar for one is getting higher.

rundown.h: The Beige Book describes an economy that's jogging, not running.
rundown.p: Only 2 of the Fed's 12 districts reported moderate growth; 4 saw slight gains and 3 saw no change. Consumer spending was flat in most districts and leaned on high earners, and every district cited higher oil prices. Five said firms are trimming staff through attrition as AI lifts productivity, a quiet drag on hiring.

rundown.h: Trading desks carried the big banks' third quarter.
rundown.p: Goldman's profit rose 29% to $5.29 billion on a 72% jump in equities trading, and Citi's climbed about 40%. JPMorgan earned $15.3 billion, up about 6% but short of the $16.3 billion forecast. Busy markets are paying the bills; the question for borrowers is whether lending appetite holds up as rates climb.

rundown.h: J.B. Hunt reports tonight, with fuel costs in the spotlight.
rundown.p: Analysts expect $1.81 a share on revenue of $3.59 billion, up 17.5% from a year ago. The company already warned in September, and Stephens expects earnings to fall 5–10% from the second quarter on driver and fuel costs. It's an early read on how carriers are absorbing expensive diesel.

dive.title: Private credit's record year, on both sides of the ledger
dive.dek: Defaults are at an all-time high and fund investors want out, but the money keeps coming in.
body: Private credit has had a strange 2026. Fitch's U.S. private credit default rate hit 6.3% over the 12 months through August, a record, up from 6.1% in July and above 6% every month since April. Meanwhile managers raised about $190 billion in the first half, 53% more than a year earlier. Lenders are cashing record checks and logging record defaults at the same time.

Look at how these loans are defaulting. Nearly half of Fitch's trailing-year default events (47%) were interest deferrals or swaps into payment-in-kind (PIK) interest, which means the borrower pays with more debt instead of cash. Another 41% were maturity extensions under stress. Actual bankruptcies and liquidations made up just 4%. So the stress is mostly being pushed into the future rather than written off. The Boston Fed estimates PIK now accounts for roughly 9.8% of BDC loans, up from about 5–6% in early 2022.

The trouble is concentrated where real estate investors should be paying attention. Industrial and manufacturing borrowers defaulted at 9.9% in August, up from 5.2% a year earlier, and transportation and distribution had two of the month's 14 default events. Small companies are hit hardest: borrowers with under $25 million of EBITDA are defaulting at 12%. Those are the mid-sized fleet, equipment and contractor businesses that rent yards and small industrial space, and their floating-rate debt isn't getting any cheaper.

The liquidity side is calmer but still awkward. In the third quarter, redemption requests at non-traded BDCs averaged 9.8% of shares, down from 10.3% in Q2 but still roughly double the usual 5% quarterly cap. Blackstone's $77 billion BCRED got $4.3 billion of requests and paid out the standard 5%. Blue Owl Technology Income Corp. saw requests worth 39% of its shares. The picture improves if PIK loans start paying cash again and defaults roll over; it gets worse if PIK keeps climbing, more funds hit their gates, or energy costs push more small industrial borrowers past the point of extend-and-pretend.

reading.title: Sam Zell sells the top: the Grave Dancer's greatest exit
reading.dek: In February 2007, a man famous for buying wreckage sold America's biggest office landlord for about $39 billion, just before the music stopped.
reading.body:
Most investors are remembered for what they bought. Sam Zell may be best remembered for something he sold. In February 2007, funds managed by Blackstone completed their purchase of Equity Office Properties, the office empire Zell had started in 1976, for roughly $39 billion, or $55.50 a share. It was the largest leveraged buyout ever at the time. Within about a year and a half, the credit markets that had paid for it were coming apart.

The odd part is that Zell made his name doing the opposite. In 1976 he wrote an article called The Grave Dancer, and the nickname followed him for the rest of his career. The idea was simple and a little morbid: when developers were choking on high interest rates and buildings were going cheap, Zell showed up as the buyer. He bought what other people had to sell, again and again through the mid-1970s recession. His instincts went back a long way. Born in Chicago in 1941 to Jewish parents who had fled Poland months earlier, he was managing apartment buildings in Ann Arbor while still a student at the University of Michigan.

So why would a buyer of distress turn seller at the peak? Because the contrarian rule isn't to always buy. It's to lean against the crowd when the crowd is paying too much or too little. By early 2007 money was cheap and plentiful, and buyers were lining up. Equity Office set off a bidding war between Blackstone and Vornado Realty Trust that the New York Times ranked as the fiercest buyout fight since RJR Nabisco in 1988, and the competition reportedly added up to $3 billion to the price. When a grave dancer finds himself at a party, he doesn't stay to admire the decorations. He collects the check. Zell personally netted about $1 billion, PBS and the AP reported.

What happened next shows how hot things had gotten. Blackstone didn't plan to sit on the whole portfolio. In the same month it closed, it sold eight buildings to affiliates of Harry Macklowe for about $7 billion. In April 2007 it sold the Washington, D.C. portfolio to Beacon Capital Partners for $6.5 billion. The buyer of the biggest deal in history was flipping pieces of it at once, at prices that only made sense in a world of easy credit. It kept selling for years, including a $3.5 billion Silicon Valley portfolio to Hudson Pacific in 2014.

Zell wasn't infallible, and the story is better for admitting it. In December 2007 he took control of Tribune in a leveraged deal financed almost entirely with debt. A year later the company filed what was then the largest bankruptcy in U.S. media history. The same man who read the cycle perfectly as a seller missed it as a buyer, a reminder that discipline has to be applied every time, not just remembered.

Zell died in May 2023 at 81. What he left investors is less a formula than a habit: notice who is eager, notice who is desperate, and ask which side of that trade you want to be on.

quote.src: Sam Zell, to The Associated Press

takeaways: Stocks are still near records and buyers are eager. Zell's lesson is that a crowded bidding room is often the best time to sell.
With the 10-year back near its highest level since 2007, deals that only work with cheap debt deserve a hard second look.
Higher rates squeeze overleveraged owners, and that pressure creates the forced sellers a grave dancer waits for. Keep some dry powder.
